Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 148 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2021) 
Background 
Alberta Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 148 (Schuler WMU) is found in the southeast of the province north of Medicine Hat. 
It covers an area of approximately 2,880 km2. This area is within the dry mixedgrass natural subregion of the province. The 
WMU encompasses land south and east of Canadian Forces Base Suffield to the TransCanada Highway (Highway 1). The 
western extent of the WMU begins at secondary highway 884 between Highway 1 and Ralston, and extends east to the 
Alberta/Saskatchewan border. The northern boundary is road allowance 18-0 (Hilda road). The main habitat features within 
the WMU include the South Saskatchewan River valley as well as several shallow lakes fed by runoff or groundwater 
(Chappice Lake, Sam Lake, Many Islands Lake, and Schuler Lake). The primary land uses in the WMU are cattle grazing and 
annual crop production. Habitat consists of native grassland (the majority of which is Crown land), tame grassland, and 
cultivated cropland. Oil and gas development is also present, and in recent years, renewable energy development has 
increased within the WMU. Chronic Wasting disease is well established within the WMU, with an overall prevalence of 34.5% 
in mule deer bucks and 16.5% in mule deer does from samples submitted in 2020. 
The established pre-hunting season population goal for WMU 148 is 1237 mule deer and 1100 white-tailed deer. Ungulate 
harvest in WMU 148 is currently managed using a special license draw for antlered and antlerless mule deer, antlerless white-
tailed deer, elk, and moose. During the archery only season, antlered white-tailed deer and mule deer are hunted with general 
licenses, which are available without the requirement of a Special License obtained through the draw process. Landowner 
licenses for mule deer and elk are also available to eligible residents. 
A survey for ungulates (mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose) was last conducted for WMU 148 in 2014 using a similar 
strip-transect methodology, thus results between 2014 and 2021 are comparable, though the 2014 survey occurred after antler 
shed. This survey resulted in an estimate of 2771 mule deer, thus the WMU was significantly over goal at that time (Table 1). 
Subsequent management was focused on lowering the population towards the established goal. 
The objective of the February 2021 survey was to assess the status of the ungulate population in WMU 148 by determining 
estimates for abundance, density and age-sex composition. We also recorded observations of additional species of game 
management or conservation concern including elk, pronghorn, carnivores, game birds, and sensitive or at risk species. 
Survey method 
A rotary wing transect survey was conducted February 11-13, 2021 flying 33 east-west lines at 1.85 km intervals, which 
obtained 43% coverage (800 m wide survey strip, area surveyed 1251 km2) for a total linear survey effort of 1564 km. At each 
observation point, ungulates were classified by species, and when possible, sex and age was recorded. Antler size for bucks 
was classified as ‘small’ (spike or two points on one or both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or more points; antlers inside 
ears), or large (antlers with ≥ 4 points, antlers outside of ears). 
Due to the variation in transect length, the average density (R; #/km2) of mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose was 
calculated by multiplying the number of animals per transect (Σx) by total area searched (total survey strip area [Σz]) (Jolly 
1969, as described in Krebs 2014). Average density (R) was multiplied by the WMU area (z) to determine the population 
estimates with a 90% confidence interval. Confidence interval width was calculated by multiplying the t statistic for the left-
tailed inverse of the Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without replacement) of the abundance 
estimate where SE=sq root variance, and variance=N*(N-n)/(n*(n-1))*(Σx2+R2*Σz2-2*R*Σxz) with N as the total number of 
possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as the number of transects sampled. 
Elk and moose observations made during the survey were recorded, though population estimates were not calculated as the 
survey method and sample obtained was not appropriate for these species.

Results 
A total of 412 mule deer were observed with an average groups size of 3 (range 1-13). The estimated density was 0.33 mule 
deer/km2 and the estimated abundance was 948 individuals (90% CI 745 – 1,151), representing a 66% decline in mule deer 
abundance since the last transect survey in 2014. A total of 360 mule deer were successfully classified and the buck:doe:fawn 
ratio was estimated to be 45:100:95. That results in an estimated 2021 winter mule deer population of 178 bucks, 395 does, 
and 375 fawns. Of the 68 mule deer bucks classified, 33 (49%) were classified ‘small’, 14 (21%) ‘medium’, and 21 (31%) 
‘large’. 
A total of 502 white-tailed deer were observed with an average group size of 6 (range 1-45). The estimated density was 0.40 
deer/km2 and the estimated abundance was 1,155 individuals (90% CI 702 – 1,609), representing a comparable result in 
white-tailed deer abundance since the last survey in 2014 (less than 1% decrease). A total of 355 white-tailed deer were 
successfully classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 7:100:84. That results in an estimated 2021 early 
winter white-tailed deer population of 42 bucks, 605 does, and 508 fawns. Of the 13 white-tailed deer bucks classified, 8 (62%) 
were classified ‘small’, 4 (31%) ‘medium’, and 1 (8%) ‘large’. 
One moose was observed during the aerial survey of WMU 148. One observation was not enough to estimate population, 
however, the result indicates there is a low density of moose within WMU 148. Twenty-five elk were also observed during the 
WMU 148 survey. Other species observed included pronghorn, sharp-tailed grouse, bald eagle, coyote, and Hungarian 
partridge.
